title: Things I am good at and things I am practising
keyIdea: Everyone has things they are good at and things they are still practising, even grown-ups. A thing you can do well every time is a thing you are good at, and it is fine to say so. A thing you can do only some of the time is a thing you are practising, not a thing you are bad at. Say “I’m practising it”, not “I’m bad at it”, and pick one small, clear goal, like “catch the ball 5 times in a row”.
familyTip: At dinner, each person names two things they are good at and one thing they are practising, grown-ups too. Say your own out loud: “I’m good at cooking. I’m practising the guitar.” If your child says “I’m bad at it”, ask “Do you mean you’re practising it?” and help them pick one small goal for the week.

visual.caption: Good at it now, or still practising? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Rides a bike with no help
Friends ask for his cat drawings
Reads a story to his sister

lab.caption: Flagship lab: sort Sam's cards, find what each person is practising, swap put-downs for kind words, pick good goals, then make your own board.

kid: Some things you can do well, every time. You ride your bike. You draw a cat. Those are things you are good at. It is fine to say so.
Some things you can do only some of the time. The ball drops. The laces come undone. Those are things you are still practising. Practising does not mean you are bad at it.
Everyone has both. Your friend swims fast but is learning to skip. Dad cooks well but is learning the guitar. Nobody is good at everything, and everybody is good at something.
Talk kindly to yourself. Say “I’m practising reading”, not “I’m bad at reading”. Then pick one small goal, like “catch the ball 5 times in a row”. Try it a little each day.
adult: Ages 6 to 7. The PSHE Association Programme of Study asks key stage 1 children to recognise what they are good at and what they find difficult, and how to manage when something is hard. The DfE Health Education guidance (2019) links self-respect and mental wellbeing. The Early Years goal for self-regulation already asks children to set and work towards simple goals. This lesson joins those up: name strengths, name one thing being practised, and turn it into a goal.

The lab uses evidence, not feelings, to sort. Can Sam do it well every time? Then he is good at it. Can he do it only some of the time? Then he is practising it. This helps children who play their strengths down, and children who label any wobble as failure. Goal research (Locke and Latham, 2002) finds that a specific goal, such as five catches in a row, works better than “do your best” or “get better”.

Common mistakes: thinking practising means being bad at it; thinking that saying “I’m good at drawing” is showing off; believing grown-ups or clever children are good at everything; saying “I’m not good at anything” after one hard day; and picking goals that are too big, vague or perfect (“never drop a ball”), or about beating others (“be the best in the class”). Be careful with praise words too: praising effort is not magic. Studies of mindset talks alone find small effects, so the real work is practice with a clear goal.

At home, name your own strengths and practising things out loud, so your child hears that grown-ups are still learning. In the lab your child sorts Sam’s cards, finds what four people are practising, swaps put-downs for kind words, chooses two good goals, and builds a board of their own.

practice.prompt: Tom can do up his coat, but the zip gets stuck most days. What is the zip for Tom?
choices: A thing he is still practising
A thing he is good at
A thing he is bad at
practice.hint: Can Tom do it well every time, or only some of the time?
practice.explain: Only some of the time, so Tom is still practising it. Practising is not the same as bad at it.

practice.prompt: Sam caught {n} balls on Monday. After a week of practice, he catches {k} more than that. How many does he catch now?
practice.hint: Start at {n} and count on {k} more.
practice.explain: {n} and {k} more make {=n+k} balls. Practice helps a thing you can’t do yet get easier.

practice.prompt: Ava says, “I’m bad at skipping.” What could she say instead?
practice.hint: Which words help her keep trying?
practice.explain: “I’m practising skipping” is true and kind. It helps Ava keep going.

practice.prompt: Leo names {n} things he is good at and {k} things he is practising. How many things are on his board?
practice.hint: Add the good-at things and the practising things together.
practice.explain: {n} and {k} make {=n+k} things. Everyone has some of both.

practice.prompt: Which is a good goal for someone practising reading?
choices: Read 1 page to Mum every night
Be the best reader in the class
practice.hint: A good goal is small and clear, and it is about your own practice.
practice.explain: Read 1 page every night is small and clear. Being the best is about beating others, and never wrong is too hard.

pool.prompt: Mia can ride her scooter fast, with no help. Is it OK for her to say, “I’m good at scooting”?
choices: No, only grown-ups can say that
pool.hint: Can Mia do it well every time?
pool.explain: Yes. Saying a true thing you are good at is not showing off. It is OK to know your strengths.

pool.hint: Think of Dad learning the guitar.
pool.explain: No. Everyone is good at some things and still practising others, even grown-ups and teachers.

pool.prompt: Kit says, “I’m not good at anything.” What is true?
choices: Everyone is good at some things
Only some children are good at things
pool.hint: Can Kit do anything well every time, like run or build?
pool.explain: Everyone is good at some things. Help Kit name two, and one thing Kit is practising.

choices: Catch the ball 5 times in a row
Write my name with no wobbly letters
pool.hint: Which one does not say what, or how much?
pool.explain: Get better is too vague: at what, and how much? A good goal is clear, like 5 catches in a row.

pool.prompt: Ella swam {n} strokes last week. Now she swims {k} more. How many strokes can she swim now?
pool.explain: {n} and {k} more make {=n+k} strokes. A little practice each day helps.

pool.prompt: Ben trips a lot when he skips. What should he do?
choices: Keep practising a little each day
Stop: he is bad at it
Only try when no one is looking
pool.hint: Do things you are practising get easier if you stop?
pool.explain: Keep practising a little each day. Tripping is part of practising, not a sign he is bad at it.

pool.prompt: Which goal is about beating other people, not your own practice?
choices: Be the best in the class
pool.hint: Which goal needs someone else to do worse?
pool.explain: Be the best in the class is about beating others, and it is not up to you. Pick a goal about your own practice.

pool.prompt: Zoe has {n} things on her good-at list and {k} on her practising list. How many more good-at things than practising things?
pool.hint: Take the practising number away from the good-at number.
pool.explain: {n} take away {k} is {=n-k}. Both lists are part of Zoe.

pool.prompt: Dad is learning to play the guitar. What does that show?
pool.hint: Do people stop learning when they grow up?
pool.explain: Grown-ups practise things too. Everyone is still learning something.
